events.title: 80 Years of Martin and Lewis: You’re Never Too Young (1955)
events.description:
A gender-swapped remake of Billy Wilder’s The Major and the Minor, this lush Technicolor vehicle combines such ludicrously cartoonish plot elements as jet-ski chase sequences, forced cigar eating, and show-stopping dance numbers. It centres on an aspiring barber (Lewis) who, mistakenly finding himself in possession of a stolen diamond, goes on the run under the assumed identity of an 11-year-old boy. When his disguise attracts the affection of a beautiful teacher (Diana Lynn) he grows determined to maintain the masquerade as long as he can. That is, until her boyfriend (Martin) arrives on the scene and proceeds to increasingly absurd comic lengths to expose his secret.

The Cahiers Du Cinema critics who famously lauded Lewis’ work in the sixties retrospectively identified You’re Never Too Young as early evidence of Lewis’s emergence as an auteur. The film also anticipates the eye-poppingly animated style largely attributed to Lewis’ collaborations with Frank Tashlin in the late fifties and early sixties.

The film will be preceded by an introduction reflecting on Martin and Lewis’s feud and break-up.
events.excerpt: You’re Never Too Young was the fourteenth of sixteen Martin and Lewis comedies released during their ten-year partnership. It was produced at the height of their highly publicised feud, when the pair were barely on speaking terms.

events.title: Extravaganza of Silent Films About Filmmaking – to Help The Cinema Museum Buy its Home
events.description:
A special Kennington Bioscope Gala Show, with all proceeds going towards our host venue the Cinema Museum to help it raise the funds to buy its building.

For our main feature, we will be screening A Girl’s Folly (1917), directed by Maurice Tourneur, and edited by future director Clarence Brown. The film shows filmmaking at Fort Lee, New Jersey, including the lab, editing room, and film sets. Variety noted ‘The public should be greatly interested in seeing how moving pictures are made – it is all here.’ Maurice Tourneur appears in front of the camera, as do an uncredited Leatrice Joy and Josef von Sternberg.

We will have a full programme of rare supporting shorts, including unseen footage of a British studio at work in 1921, a tinted 35mm print of Hello Hollywood (1927), Chaplin’s Kid Auto Races at Venice (1914) in which we see the birth of the Tramp character, a short film taking us behind the scenes of French productions of 1929 and the world premiere of Dave Glass’s brand new restoration of the rare Snub Pollard film In the Movies (1922) – plus anything else we can cram in!

We will also have some antique 35mm movie cameras from the silent era on display.

This special evening will showcase both filmmaking and film exhibition, to provide a completely unique evening celebrating making and screening films during the silent era – all in aid of the only museum in London dedicated to the golden age of the cinema.

Live piano accompaniment. Ashley Valentine will be playing for A Girl’s Folly, and Colin Sell and John Sweeney will be playing for the shorts in the first half.
events.excerpt: All proceeds of this Kennington Bioscope Gala go to the Cinema Museum appeal! Featuring Maurice Tourneur’s A Girl’s Folly (1917), set in a New Jersey film studio, with a full supporting programme of rare shorts, including Chaplin, Feuillade and the world premiere of a new restoration of a rare Snub Pollard film!

events.title: Away Up North – An Evening Of Movie Mavericks from Finland
events.description:
After its milestone 40th anniversary, the legendary Midnight Sun Film Festival makes a one-off pilgrimage to the home of film history, the Cinema Museum in London. Founded in the Finnish Arctic Circle by Director brothers Aki and Mika Kaurismäki, the renowned international film festival has been exciting movie fans at the top of the world for decades.

London will be treated to a showcase of films curated from the vaults of the Finnish Film Archive. In the true spirit of the festival that never sleeps, there will be new discoveries and contemporary classics from Finnish mavericks. The highlight will be live accompaniment by notable Finnish musicians Lau Nau and Henri Utan K. This continues the festival’s long legacy of reinterpreting silent cinema with fresh, contemporary live scores.

The evening closes with a rare 35mm screening of Mika Kaurismäki’s wisecracking cult film The Liar (1981), written and starring his brother Aki. It is preceded by Aki’s tribute to the Lumiére brothers, The Foundry (2007) and festival favourite Finnish Frustrations (1969), a groundbreaking feminist short by Eila Kaarresalo-Kasari.

Tervetuloa – a warm welcome.

7PM: INTRO

Midnight Sun Film Festival (Heikki Ortamo, 1987, 9min)

The greatest film festival (anti-)promotional short ever made, which explains why Midnight Sun is a unique event for both Finnish film buffs and some of the stellar international talents who attend it. The latter also appear in this hilarious guide to a very Finland way of sharing films.

Format: 35mm.

7.15 PM: PART ONE

Jean Sibelius at Home (Aho & Soldan, 1927, 6 min) – live score by Lau Nau

Late autumn, 1927, at the home of maestro Jean Sibelius in Ainola, Finland. A charming, little, free-form documentary about Sibelius and his family celebrating an autumn day. Heidi and Margareta Sibelius play four-hand piano, Aino is busy in the garden, the morning papers and a cigar start the master’s day. A classic from Finnish documentary pioneers Heikki Aho and Björn Soldan.

Format 16mm.

Once Upon Time There Was Winter – and Snow (Unknown,1934, 6 min) – live score by Lau Nau

The Finnish realm of snow and ice. In this unknown gem from almost a century ago, the progress of an icebreaker ship feels like a symbol of the modernisation and urbanisation of the world: slow but inevitable. The relationship with nature is still carefree. Joys of winter are taken for granted, and the urban core of Finland produces images that may seem like a fairytale to an outsider. Greetings from a time of innocence.

Format: DCP.

Varala, Women’s Paradise (Aimo Jäderholm, 1947, 9 min) – live score by Henri Utan K

Summer 1947, a poetic, skillfully rhythmic documentary about Varala, the legendary women’s physical education institute. Located in a scenic peninsula on the shores of Lake Pyhäjärvi, it is the pride of Finland’s second city, Tampere. For decades Varala has been a haven for women’s sports. “Even though we only appear to be playing, we are doing it for the good of the fatherland.”

Format: 16mm.

Rocky VI (Aki Kaurismäki, 1986, 9 min)

A musical parody of Rocky IV (1985) topped with Aki Kaurismäki’s singular deadpan humour. Rocky, played by Silu Seppänen of Leningrad Cowboys fame, defends the Free World and battles the hulking Siberian boxer, Igor. Has Rocky finally met his match?

Format: 35mm.

A Planet Far Away (Juha Kuosmanen, 2023, 16 min) – live score by Lau Nau & Henri Utan K

Using handmade trickery, silent cinema is reawakened with a modern twist. From the Cannes-winning director Juho Kuosmanen (Compartment No. 6), the final instalment of the celebrated silent trilogy tells a story of lighthouse-keeper Marlanda and her little brother Maximilian. It’s a bedtime story about the end of everything and the extraordinary attempts to survive it. But it’s not bedtime, it’s just the interval.

Format: DCP.

8:15 PM: INTERMISSION

8:30 PM: PART TWO

The Foundry (Aki Kaurismäki, 2007, 4 min)

Another proletarian life slice, this time set in Karkkila, hometown of director Aki Kaurismäki. Workers at a foundry eat their lunch while watching the Lumiére brothers’ film La Sortie de l’usine Lumière à Lyon (1895).

Format: DCP.

Finnish Frustrations (Eila Kaarresalo-Kasari, 1969, 7 min)

Diminishing dances. The last chance for women and men to find a partner. In seven minutes, this feminist cornerstone of Finnish cinema isolates an aspect of sexual inequality with a narrative starkness.

Format: DCP.

The Liar (Mika Kaurismäki, 1981, 53 min)

Mika Kaurismäki’s debut film set the tone for his groundbreaking Finnish cinema of the following decades. Ville Alfa (Aki Kaurismäki) is a lazy, young student vainly trying to finish his first proletarian novel. He likes to walk the streets of Helsinki, tell stories, spin lies and scam money off his friends. All for more drink and more women. Then one day, he meets Tuula (Pirkko Hämäläinen) and tries to change. A witty tribute to Jean-Luc Godard, and a delightful discovery for many.

Format: 35mm.

Total duration: approx. 2.5 hours including interval.

MUSICIANS

Lau Nau

Lau Nau, AKA Laura Naukkarinen, is a Finnish composer and sound artist whose music is imbued with an idiosyncratic, finely honed, sonic world view. Her palette often consists of traditional instruments, singing voice, modular synthesisers and field recordings.

Releasing albums on record labels in Europe, US and Japan, Lau Nau has toured internationally for 25 years. Venues such as the Castro Theatre in San Francisco, Super Deluxe in Tokyo, and NYC’s Knitting Factory have all welcomed her music. Lau Nau has played live accompaniment to silent films at festivals such as Midnight Sun Film Festival, San Francisco Silent Film Festival and Bologna’s Il Cinema Ritrovato.

Henri Utan K

Henri Utan K [ˈhɛn⟨r⟩ɪ uːtʌn kɒ] is the moniker of Finnish-born, London-based experimental guitarist and composer Henri Växby. On the fringes of the new music scene since the early 00s, his work moves between part-improvisation and full composition, combining stark dissonance with gently hypnotic soundscapes and ambient drones.

Henri studied composition at Goldsmiths University under Prof. Roger Redgate and at City St George’s University under Dr Claudia Molitor. He has been featured on BBC 6 Music, BBC Radio 3, at the Rainy Days Festival and Cafe OTO. Henri is also co-leader of avant-pop duo French For Cartridge and Finnish, post-Beatles outfit Icons of Elegance.

The event is supported by the Finnish Institute in the UK and Ireland.

events.title: Closed Circuit (1978)
events.description:
A matinee showing of a spaghetti western becomes a whodunnit a a member of the audience is shot dead during the gunslinging showdown.

The Cinema of Tomorrow (F.K.A. PEPCOT) presents the second of three screenings on the theme of ‘Movies at the Movies’. Closed Circuit (1978) was made for Italian TV, but has since become a beloved cult hit for its mix of murder mystery and a sincere and philosophical love of the ‘magic’ of cinema. Come and watch Closed Circuit as it was never intended, but where it deserves to be, up on the big screen.

This event is part of Programmers of Tomorrow (PoT): A season of workshops and screenings for the future of film exhibition. Consisting of two free workshops, three fundraiser screenings and a film festival all-dayer, PoT is spreading knowledge about film programming, building community around the love of movies, and facilitating first timers to put on their first ever public screening! Read more about it and how to get involved here.

This screening is a fundraiser for both PoT and its venue, The Cinema Museum. The Cinema Museum is currently raising money to buy its amazing building and cement its place as the living archive of London’s cinema history.

Doors will open at 6.30pm for drinks and snacks amidst the ephemera of cinemas past, showtime at 7.30pm!

events.title: Dyn Amo (1973) on 16mm
events.description:
The Cinema Museum is proud to present a series of avant-garde film screenings on 16mm in benefit of the Museum’s fundraiser to buy our home.

Our third screening of the season is Dyn Amo (1973), by the avant-garde filmmaker Stephen Dwoskin.

An early work of feminist cinema, associated with Laura Mulvey’s ‘gaze theory’:

“Dyn Amo is a ‘drama’ exploring the distinction between a person’s self and his projection of that self to others; and it’s a ‘horror movie’ tragically suggesting how a projection can become more substantial than the self behind it. Its subjects are role-playing (especially sexual role-playing), and the masochism of playing a role that conforms to others’ exploitative interests.” Tony Rayns

The screening will be introduced by Rachel Garfield, co-editor of Dwoskino: The Gaze of Stephen Dwoskin (LUX, 2022) and the forthcoming Stephen Dwoskin is… (published by BFI).

All proceeds from this screening will go towards the Museum’s fundraiser to buy our home.
events.excerpt: Dyn Amo (1973), by the avant-garde filmmaker Stephen Dwoskin, is an early work of feminist cinema, associated with Laura Mulvey’s ‘gaze theory’.

events.title: Murders in the Zoo (1933) and Shivers (1975)
events.description:
Murders in the Zoo opens our new season in fine style, with one of favourite villains (the suavely incomparable Lionel Atwill) playing an insanely jealous big-game hunter who plots to ‘dispose’ of his beautiful but unfaithful wife’s lovers. And he just happens to own a private zoo…

This is one of those dark ‘pre-Code’, anything-goes horrors that we love at the Gothique, with no less a critic than Leonard Maltin calling it “astonishingly grisly”!

Following that opener, we are delighted to present our main feature ‘partly’ on 35mm, courtesy of the Cinema Museum’s extensive film collection: ‘partly’ because one of the 35mm reels is missing, so the ‘gap’ will be filled by a digital copy. But it’s still lovely to wheel out the ‘old technology’ from time to time!

Shivers (also known as The Parasite Murders) was celebrated director David Cronenberg’s first foray into feature production, following a series of largely experimental short films. It heralded his fascination with ‘body horror’, with a scientist experimenting, in an up-market apartment complex, with the use of genetically-engineered parasites as organ transplants.

But the parasites combine aphrodisiac with VD… and, as a suspicious doctor begins an investigation, residents start showing signs that they are spreading rapidly, in an extremely unpleasant manner.
events.excerpt: The new Gothique Film Society season starts with a pre-Code horror and the feature debut of celebrated ‘body horror’ director David Cronenberg.

events.title: Programmers of Tomorrow Workshop #2 – Licenses & Community with Token Homo
events.description:
Programmers of Tomorrow’s second (and final) workshop is facilitated by the brilliant, energetic and endlessly creative film programmer Token Homo – if you haven’t been to his Bar Trash (opens in a new window) events at cinemas across London, you haven’t lived. The workshop will start with the practical with a brief breakdown of the basics of film licensing, and then get down to the juicy creative stuff. You’ll hear from Richard aka Token Homo about how and why he builds queer community around the beauty of the B-movie, and get the chance to bounce your own community film programming ideas and dreams around with other film lovers. All amidst the ephemera of cinemas past at the beautiful Cinema Museum!

Doors will open at 12.15pm. The workshop will begin at 1pm and run until 3pm, with a short break in the middle.

Apply to screen your film of choice at the Programmers of Tomorrow all-dayer!
Programmers of Tomorrow culminates in an all-day triple-feature film-festival at the Cinema Museum on Sun 29 November, where every programmer screens a film for the first time! You don’t have you attend any PoT workshops in order to submit your idea for the PoT all-dayer, but they can be a great space to develop your idea! All-dayer submission form coming soon, deadline Sun 25 Oct. If selected, you will have access to funding to pay for film licensing and support with promoting your screening.

If you have any other questions or requests please do get in touch!
cinemaoftomorrowldn@gmail.com

events.title: The Mothman Prophecies (2002)
events.description:
Journalist John Klein (Richard Gere) is involved in a car accident where his wife (Laura Linney) claims to have seen a moth-like creature suddenly appear in front of them.

Klein decides to investigate of other reported sightings, which takes him to Point Pleasant, West Virginia, where sightings and experiences appear to be concentrated.

Based on actual events which took place between 1966 and 1967, The Mothman Prophecies (2002) is a unique, tense and unusual paranormal thriller, and Richard Gere is excellent in this hugely underrated film.

Presented and introduced by Jacknoir. At the end of the film, Jacknoir will give a short talk entitled ” The Mothman Debunked?”.
events.excerpt: After a life changing accident where his wife mentions seeing a moth like creature appear in front of their car, journalist John Klein (Richard Gere) conducts a personal investigation into The Mothman. A tense paranormal thriller based on true events which occurred in and around a small town in West Virginia.

events.title: Force of Evil (1948)
events.description:
Director Abraham Polonsky, and starring John Garfield, Thomas Mitchell, Marie Windsor and Beatrice Pearson. Digital presentation.

Unscrupulous New York lawyer Joe Morse (John Garfield) has the opportunity to make it big by teaming up with a cutthroat gangster to consolidate a numbers racket. The only hitch is Morse’s brother refuses to involve his bank in the plan.

Having received an Oscar nomination for his script of Body and Soul (1947), Polonsky also wrote the script of his directorial debut. Having produced one of the high points of the film noir genre, he fell foul, like his star, of the House Un-American Activities Committee. Refusing to “name names”, he was blacklisted. After 21 years, he finally directed his second feature, Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here (1969). Then, while directing his next film Romance of a Horsethief (1971), he developed a severe heart problem, and after surgery was advised not to direct again. One of the great might-have-beens of Hollywood.

events.title: The Hart of London (1970) on 16mm
events.description:
The Cinema Museum is proud to present a series of avant-garde film screenings on 16mm in benefit of the Museum’s fundraiser to buy our home.

Our fourth screening of the season is The Hart of London (1970), by Canadian experimental filmmaker Jack Chambers.

Praised by Stan Brakhage as “one of the greatest films ever made”, The Hart of London is shown in black and white and colour, and includes found news footage from 1954, film shot by the artist years earlier in Spain, and film shot by the artist in London, Ontario. The film is preoccupied with the tensions between nature and the city of London: “It explores life and death, the sense of place and personal displacement, and the intricate aesthetics of representation. It is a personal and spiritual film, marked inevitably by Chambers’ knowledge that he had leukemia.”
​
The Cinema Museum is proud this screening of this rare avant-garde film on 16mm, as benefit to the Museum’s fundraiser to buy our home.

The film is preoccupied with the tensions between nature and the city of London.

events.title: The Arrival from the Darkness (Príchozí z temnot) (1921)
events.description:
Digital restoration. Director Jan S. Kolár 1921 – Czech. Featuring Theodor Pistek, Anny Ondra, Josef Svab.

A 1921 supernatural fantasy from Czechoslovakia which follows a collector who revives his 16th-century ancestor using an ancient manuscript and the Elixir of Life, unleashing a gothic tale involving alchemy, plague-era mysticism, ruined castles, and occult rituals. Shot at Czech castles and historic locations, the film also showcases the work of cinematographers Otto Heller and Otto Hoffmann. Heller would later become a major figure in British cinema, photographing films including The Ladykillers and Peeping Tom.

Director Jan S. Kolár, born in Prague in 1896, was among the defining figures of the Czech silent era, working as a director, screenwriter, actor, and producer during the industry’s formative years in that country. The cast includes Theodor Pistek, Josef Svab and Anny Ondra, remembered as the heroine of Hitchcock’s Blackmail, (she was seen previously in Kennington Bioscope’s 2019 presentation of the 1927 Czech comedy An Old Gangster’s Molls).

events.title: Night of the Comet (1984)
events.description:
Where in LA do you wait out the apocalypse? The cinema and the shopping mall of course!

The Cinema of Tomorrow (F.K.A PEPCOT) presents the final of three screenings on the theme of ‘Movies at the Movies’. Night of the Comet (1984) is a sci-fi zom-com about sisterhood that whirls ecstatically across a lusciously depicted and (almost) empty Los Angeles. The characters of sisters Regina and Samantha Belmont were frequently cited by the creators of Buffy the Vampire Slayer – they are the quick-quipping, ass-kicking, fashion-forward blueprints. Roger Ebert and Gene Siskel agreed, throwing a big two thumbs up at this grade-A B-movie. 👍👍

This event is part of Programmers of Tomorrow (PoT): A season of workshops and screenings for the future of film exhibition. Consisting of two free workshops, three fundraiser screenings and a film festival all-dayer, PoT is spreading knowledge about film programming, building community around the love of movies, and facilitating first timers to put on their first ever public screening! Read more about it and how to get involved here.

This screening is a fundraiser for both PoT and its venue, The Cinema Museum. The Cinema Museum is currently raising money to buy its amazing building and cement its place as the living archive of London’s cinema history.

Doors will open at 6.30pm for drinks and snacks amidst the ephemera of cinemas past, showtime at 7.30pm!

events.title: The Beast (2023)
events.description:
Bertrand Bonello’s The Beast follows Gabrielle (Léa Seydoux), a woman living in a near future where artificial intelligence has come to dominate society and human emotions are considered a threat. To rid herself of her feelings, she undergoes a procedure that takes her back through her previous lives. Across three different eras — Paris in 1910, Los Angeles in 2014 and a dystopian 2044 — she repeatedly encounters Louis (George MacKay), a mysterious man with whom she shares an inexplicable connection.

Loosely inspired by Henry James’s The Beast in the Jungle, Bonello’s film is a haunting exploration of love, fear and the anticipation of catastrophe. Its shifting identities, uncanny repetitions and ominous Los Angeles evoke the worlds of Mulholland Drive and Lost Highway, while its anxieties about artificial intelligence and the suppression of emotion bring the Lynchian into a distinctly contemporary setting. As the concluding film in Not By Lynch, The Beast offers a vision of a world in which the desire to escape fear threatens to extinguish the very possibility of human connection.

With an introduction and accompanying commissioned essay, presented in collaboration with Cinema Year Zero.

categories.name: Not By Lynch
categories.description: Not By Lynch: The Lynchian Before and After David Lynch - is a nine-film programme paying tribute to the late David Lynch by exploring films that share aspects of his distinctive style and sensibility. Like any great artist, Lynch not only imprinted his unique vision on the world but also examined it with a discerning eye. The collision between that subjective vision and the objective reality gave rise to what we now call the 'Lynchian': a perspective in which everyday reality is a thin veil over a dream-state that feels closer to the truth. While this vision finds its most intense and sustained expression in Lynch’s own films, the Lynchian both predates Lynch and will survive him, so long as the world that inspired it endures. Beginning 16 January 2026 - one year after Lynch’s death - the programme unfolds across nine decades of his lifetime (1940s–2020s), pairing precursors and descendants that echo the moods, methods, and mysteries we call Lynchian. Each screening will be preceded by an introduction and accompanied by an original commissioned essay, produced by Cinema Year Zero. The season is curated by Arta Barzanji. (Links open in new tabs).

events.title: Home Movie Day 2026
events.description:
Don’t throw your films away; bring them to Home Movie Day!

“Saving our film heritage should not be limited only to commercially produced films. Home movies do not just capture the important private moments of our family’s lives, but they are historical and cultural documents as well. Home Movie Day is a celebration of these films and the people who shot them. I urge anyone with an interest in learning more about how to care for and preserve their own personal memories to join in the festivities being offered in their community…”— Martin Scorsese

This year sees the 24th anniversary of Home Movie Day and we’ll be celebrating in true archive film style! This event is free, open to the public, and promises a day filled with nostalgia, education, and camaraderie.

Film archivists will take time out of the vaults to help the public enjoy and save their home movies. Home Movie Day shows how home movies on 8mm, Super8, 9.5mm and 16mm offer a unique view of past life in London and of family history.

It’s a family-friendly event, and everyone is welcome to attend. But remember, you don’t need to bring a film to participate fully in the day’s activities!

Join us on October 24, 2026, from 10.30 to 16.00.

Entry is absolutely free.

To make the day even sweeter, tea and cake will be available for all attendees.
events.excerpt: The annual event celebrating amateur film returns. Bring any film on 9.5 mm, super 8, 8 mm or 16 mm for a free examination by a professional film archivist followed by projection on the big screen.

events.title: Lisa Gornick in Conversation with Caroline Cassin
events.description:
Join British filmmaker, artist, and performer Lisa Gornick in conversation with curator Caroline Cassin. Celebrating Lisa’s 60th birthday, this special event will explore her expansive body of work, looking back on her filmmaking life as she embarks on a new feature film.

Lisa’s career as a filmmaker spans three decades, during which they have made three feature films and seven short films. She is celebrated for the BFI-acclaimed Do I Love You? (2002), the first British lesbian feature film in a decade (below), Tick Tock Lullaby (2007), a comedy-drama about the ambivalence around whether to be a parent and The Book of Gabrielle (2016), their first cross-platform production about talking, writing and drawing sex.

Caroline will explore with Lisa the very intimate, existential investigations that form the basis of her work. Made largely outside conventional production structures, their films have always been poignant, personal, comedic and defiantly DIY.

The evening will weave together clips from Lisa’s films, an interactive live drawing performance, music and conversation.

All proceeds from ticket sales will support two important crowdfunding campaigns: Lisa’s film and The Cinema Museum’s effort to secure its home.

5-6pm: Arrival and gathering to Lisa’s soundtrack
Doors open at 5pm, when refreshments and snacks will be available in our licensed cafe/bar; you can browse the bookstore, all soundtracked by Lisa’s favourite tunes.

6-7.15pm: Lisa Gornick in Conversation with Caroline Cassin
Lisa and Caroline explore a selection of Lisa’s chosen film clips and share stories about Lisa’s life as a filmmaker and the making of the films.

7.30-8pm: Live drawing performance
Lisa takes to the drawing table for a live, interactive drawing session, bringing the evening’s conversation into the present and giving the audience a chance to participate.

8-9pm: Birthday celebrations
More music and conversation. Maybe even dancing?

After 9pm, for those who want to keep the party going, we’ll head to another venue.

events.title: Festen (1998) on 35mm
events.description:
Festen (The Celebration), 1998, Denmark.

Following a patriarch’s lavish birthday gathering that descends into chaos, Festen lays bare the fractures beneath a façade of bourgeois respectability, rendered through handheld camerawork, stark natural lighting, and raw, unflinching performances. Winner of the Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival, this bold film announced Thomas Vinterberg as an exciting new voice at the dawn of the Dogme 95 movement.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: A Tribute to Ray Harryhausen, including The Beast from 20,000 Fathoms (1953)
events.description:
We are delighted that artist/sculptor Al Friswell, who is also the conserver of the wonderful creatures created by effects maestro Ray Harryhausen, will be joining us this evening.

Al will begin with an extensive presentation about Ray’s life and career, and will then introduce one of Ray’s earliest films, the classic Beast from 20,000 Fathoms, in which, in the Arctic, a series of atom bomb blasts causes ‘something’ to stir to life…

In a career spanning more than 40 years, Ray built upon the techniques of his mentor, Willis H. O’Brien (famous for the original 1933 King Kong), to develop a form of stop-motion animation known as ‘Dynamation’. He showcased this in a series of celebrated films such as It Came from Beneath the Sea (1955), The 7th Voyage of Sinbad (1958), The Valley of Gwangi (1969), The Golden Voyage of Sinbad (1973) and Clash of the Titans (1981). Al will cover these, and much more, in his fully illustrated presentation.

events.title: Gentlemen Among Themselves (Die fidele Herrenpartie) (1929)
events.description:
BFI 35mm print. Directed by Rudolf Walther-Fein with Hermann Picha, Lydia Potechina, Maria Paudler, Lyndia Potechina, Truus Van Aalten and Walter Rillan.

Kennington Bioscope presents Gentlemen Among Themselves, a 1929 German comedy directed by Vienna-born Rudolf Walther-Fein, who began his career as an actor. He made his stage debut aged 17 in Iglau – a German-speaking region now part of the Czech Republic – and went on to appear in cities that included Vienna, Salzburg, Munich and, finally, Berlin. It was there, in 1919, that he first obtained work as a screenwriter and director. During the 1920s, Walther-Fein directed numerous films while simultaneously serving as a production manager for the Aafa-Film company and also taking on the role of artistic supervisor for other productions. His films were mostly comedies or romantic dramas, among them 1929’s Dich hab’ ich geliebt (It’s You I Have Loved or Because I Loved You), Germany’s first all-talking feature film.

Gentlemen Among Themselves was filmed at the Staaken Studios in Berlin with sets designed by Botho Hoefer and Hans Minzloff. The story, by Franz Rauch, is of a woman warning her husband that his forthcoming stag party will be his last. Because he and his friends are determined to make the most of it, things get out of hand and the husband is knocked unconscious and his engraved lighter stolen. The lighter is subsequently used to identify a thief and the now-sober reveller believes himself to be a wanted man. Husband and wife are played by Hermann Picha and Lydia Potechina, with Maria Paudler as their daughter and Walter Rilla as her erstwhile suitor.
events.excerpt: A comedy in which Lydia Potechina (Brunhilde) warns husband Hermann Picha (Peter) that this is the last stag party he’s going to go to, so he and his friends plan to make quite a night of it. He celebrates by hitting his head against a column, knocking himself out, and getting his engraved cigarette case stolen. When this is used to identify the thief, she and daughter Maria Paudler (Wally) are distraught. Meanwhile, Picha hides out in the bad part of town.

events.title: Silent Laughter Weekend 2026
events.description:
It’s big! It’s back! And it’s better than ever!!!

Kennington Bioscope’s Silent Laughter Weekend 2026 is returning to its normal weekend length AND this year it promises to be absolutely jam-packed with wonderful comedic treasures.

As well as icons like Laurel & Hardy, Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, Harry Langdon and Harold Lloyd, our programme takes a deep dive into the world of silent comedy. As always, we’ll be spotlighting unjustly forgotten performers like Marie Prevost, Max Linder, Charley Chase, Lloyd Hamilton and Anita Garvin: you might just find your new favourite silent comedian!

This year we’re also showcasing several films celebrating their centenary; as you’ll see, 1926 was a GREAT year for film comedy. There will be rarities, premieres and showings on real celluloid. All programmes feature live music from the UK’s top accompanists, and will have engaging introductions from silent film authors, enthusiasts, collectors and historians. So, without further ado, here’s the full programme:

SATURDAY

10.00 Madame Behave (1925)

Following the great success of cross-dressing comedy Charley’s Aunt (shown last year at KB) in 1925, producer Al Christie followed up with a film starring the celebrated female impersonator Julian Eltinge. This showing is a rare chance to see Eltinge strut his stuff, alongside a great comedy cast. This screening will include newly scanned 35mm elements from the Library of Congress, enabling us to present a partial restoration of the film.

11.30 Focus On… Joker

Continuing our series of spotlights on some of the forgotten comedy studios, this time we’re very pleased to present an introduction to the world of Joker Comedies. Presented by Thomas Reeder, author of a new book about the studio, the programme will showcase rare comedy treats featuring Louise Fazenda, Bobby Vernon, Gale Henry, Billy Franey, Milburn Morante, Lillian Peacock, Max Asher, Harry McCoy, Dot Farley and Lon Chaney.

13.00 Lunch

14.00 Silent Comedy Teams

Laurel & Hardy might be the best-loved silent comedy team, but they weren’t the first, and far from the only one. Silent comedy enthusiast Matthew Ross presents a deep dive into the history of silent double (and triple!) acts. Expect clips and classic shorts featuring John Bunny & Flora Finch, Roscoe Arbuckle & Buster Keaton, ‘A Ton of Fun’, Anita Garvin & Marion Byron (pictured), and more. And of course, we have to feature Mr Laurel & Mr Hardy! Wrong Again (1929) is one of their most off-beat comedies, in which – through a series of misunderstandings – they find themselves coaxing a horse on top of a grand piano!

15.45 Hot Water (1924) and Saturday Afternoon (1926)

Two short – but perfectly formed – mini feature films. Harry Langdon’s Saturday Afternoon is a sweet-natured domestic comedy that sees innocent Harry led astray by his friend Vernon Dent. Langdon’s pantomimic gifts are given full reign in this three reel comedy. Hot Water is one of Harold Lloyd’s less well-remembered films, but contains some brilliant set pieces, including one of his funniest: Harold’s attempts to bring a live turkey home on a tramcar!

17.30 1926: It Was a Very Good Year

It’s the centenary of a golden year for silent comedy. Join silent comedy experts Glenn Mitchell and Dave Glass as they present a selection of the very best short comedies from 1926. Expect classics starring Lloyd Hamilton, Billy Bevan, Kennington Bioscope favourite Charley Chase, and more.

19.00 Dinner

20.00 King of the Circus (1924)

The great Max Linder laid the template for the great screen comedians, and Charlie Chaplin cited him as a major influence. He died tragically young at the age of 41 in 1925, but made a handful of feature films before he left us.

King of the Circus, his last film, has long been unavailable but has now been lovingly restored; we’re delighted and very proud to host its UK premiere as part of Silent Laughter Weekend.

Introduced (digitally) by Serge Bromberg, who reconstructed and restored the film.

SUNDAY

10.00 The 28MM Comedy Show

28mm was an early attempt to create a show-at-home film gauge for amateurs. Later made obsolete by 9.5 and 16mm films, it existed long enough to preserve some otherwise lost comedies. At this very special showing, film collector Christopher Bird will present some of these rare comedies on celluloid, using a 28mm projector. Make sure you’re here early on Sunday to catch this unique event, a feast of gloriously archaic analogue technology and extremely rare comedy films on real film!

11.45 The Caveman (1926)

Marie Prevost was one of the great silent comediennes, excelling at portraying sexy, sassy, strong women. In The Caveman, she’s rich and bored of the oh-so polite gentlemen she’s been dating. So, as a project, she decides to transform tough coalman Matt Moore into a man-about-town. This silent rom-com, a gender-reversed precursor to My Fair Lady, is a delight, featuring wonderful performances from Prevost and Moore. We’re proud to be showing the UK premiere of this new restoration, introduced by Michelle Facey.

13.00 Lunch

14.00 Those TV Shows…

In the 1950s and 60s, renewed interest in silent comedies saw several TV shows devoted to showcasing them: Golden Silents, Comedy Capers, Mad Movies… How many do you remember? For many of us, these programmes were our first introduction to the world of silent laughter. Dave Glass gets nostalgic as he digs into the stories behind these programmes. Featuring lots of clips (and an occasional, annoyingly catchy theme tune…)

16.00 Atta Boy (1926)

Another 1926 gem from our favourite Italian comic, little Monty Banks. Made on the heels of his classic Play Safe (1927), Atta Boy (left) sees Monty on fine form as a would-be reporter investigating a kidnapping. Featuring lots of great gags, and one of Banks’ patented stunt sequences – hanging from a ladder atop a speeding car – as a climax. Big-screen premiere of a new restoration.

17.30 Rarities & Rediscoveries

Now a regular fixture in the Silent Laughter programme, once more we’ve dug through the film collections and archives to present a programme of long-lost and forgotten funnies. What’s on the menu? Well, we’re still finalising the details, but expect the premiere of a hilarious, newly restored Snub Pollard comedy for starters, plus films starring Roscoe ‘Fatty’ Arbuckle, Larry Semon and lots more rarities that you won’t see anywhere else!

19.00 Dinner

20.00 The General – Special Centenary Showing

We couldn’t celebrate the great comedies of 1926 without including a film often considered the best silent comedy of all: Buster Keaton’s The General. This classic railroad chase comedy, set during the American Civil War, is beautifully filmed, directed and acted, and chock full of great stunts and gags. The perfect culmination to a weekend of Silent Laughter. If you’ve never seen The General on the big screen before, then there’s no better place than in the evocative surroundings of the Cinema Museum. If you have, well, you won’t want to miss the extra rare Keaton goodies that we’ll be showing to make this an extra special screening… Presented by David McLeod, of The Blinking Buzzards, the UK Buster Keaton Appreciation Society.

events.title: Chris Lewis presents: Jerry Lewis’s Home Movies, plus Q&A
events.description:
This special screening will be presented by Chris Lewis, son of Jerry Lewis and president of the American Wheelchair Mission. It will be followed by a Q&A.

About Chris Lewis:
Chris always wanted to be like his dad, Jerry Lewis, but not as a comedian. He first volunteered at the Muscular Dystrophy Association Telethon in 1972 and worked with his dad each year for 39 years. (Jerry raised over $2.5 Billion dollars for neuromuscular research and family services over 60 years.)

Chris attended film school and assisted his dad in the film editing room at their home. He worked on film sets when Jerry directed Telethon promotional spots and sat in on his production meetings. Chris was eager to learn what Jerry did and how he did it.

He road and stage managed Jerry in the 1980s, and created Jerry Lewis Comedy Classics in 1995 to distribute Jerry’s film and television assets. In early 2000, came the opportunity to create a wheelchair delivery charity assisting people in need of mobility worldwide. As President and CEO of the American Wheelchair Mission, Chris’s team delivers free wheelchairs to people praying for mobility. Since 2000, he has been involved in providing over 900,000 wheelchairs to people in more than 150 countries.

Chris wrote a book entitled Jerry Lewis on Being a Person to showcase his dad’s love of humanity, incredible talent, groundbreaking innovations, and a legacy of philanthropy that continues to improve our world. In the Foreword to Chris’s book, Jerry says about his son, “I consider him my legacy, and that makes me feel good.”

About the programme:
More than a decade before his directorial debut, The Bellboy (1960), Jerry Lewis had already begun writing and directing his close friends in a series of
16mm home movie productions, complete with synchronised sound and professional acting.

This programme offers a whistle-stop tour of highlights from these home movie productions, including the full films An Eye For An Eye and Fairfax Avenue, excerpts from parties and premieres at Lewis’s Pacific Palisades home, and more.

Before the screening, Chris Lewis will be signing copies of his book Jerry Lewis on Being a Person. A selection of ‘Save The Cinema Museum’ supporter ticket options, including a pre-show book signing and The Nutty Professor posters (each signed by Jerry Lewis and accompanied by a certificate of authenticity), are available to buy in advance and on the night. All proceeds from sales of books and posters will support The Cinema Museum’s campaign to secure its permanent home.

Organised and moderated by I’ll Say She Is curator Charlotte Ross. With special thanks to Chris Lewis (American Wheelchair Mission) and Rob Stone (Moving Image Curator, The Library of Congress).

events.title: Chris Lewis presents: The Nutty Professor (1963)
events.description:
This special screening will be presented by Chris Lewis, son of Jerry Lewis and president of the American Wheelchair Mission. It will be preceded by an introduction and followed by a Q&A.

About Chris Lewis:
Chris always wanted to be like his dad, Jerry Lewis, but not as a comedian. He first volunteered at the Muscular Dystrophy Association Telethon in 1972 and worked with his dad each year for 39 years. (Jerry raised over $2.5 Billion dollars for neuromuscular research and family services over 60 years.)

Chris attended film school and assisted his dad in the film editing room at their home. He worked on film sets when Jerry directed Telethon promotional spots and sat in on his production meetings. Chris was eager to learn what Jerry did and how he did it. He road and stage managed Jerry in the 1980s, and created Jerry Lewis Comedy Classics in 1995 to distribute Jerry’s film and television assets. In early 2000, came the opportunity to create a wheelchair delivery charity assisting people in need of mobility worldwide. As President and CEO of the American Wheelchair Mission, Chris’s team delivers free wheelchairs to people praying for mobility. Since 2000, he has been involved in providing over 900,000 wheelchairs to people in more than 150 countries.
​
Chris wrote a book entitled Jerry Lewis on Being a Person to showcase his dad’s love of humanity, incredible talent, groundbreaking innovations, and a legacy of philanthropy that continues to improve our world. In the Foreword to Chris’s book, Jerry says about his son, “I consider him my legacy, and that makes me feel good.”

About the Programme:
In this riotous spin on Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, a klutzy chemistry professor concocts a formula that transforms him into a swaggering crooner. But the effect is only ever temporary and, tempted by the newfound confidence of his alter ego, he soon finds himself struggling to keep his competing personalities under control.

Widely regarded as Jerry Lewis’s masterpiece, The Nutty Professor is a hysterical, self-reflexive portrait of fractured identity: the fullest expression of a fascination with duality that runs throughout Lewis’s work.

Before the screening, Chris Lewis will be signing copies of his book Jerry Lewis on Being a Person. A selection of ‘Save The Cinema Museum’ supporter ticket options, including a pre-show book signing and The Nutty Professor posters (each signed by Jerry Lewis and accompanied by a certificate of authenticity), are available to buy in advance and on the night. All proceeds from sales of books and posters will support The Cinema Museum’s campaign to secure its permanent home.

events.title: On Dangerous Ground (1951)
events.description:
Director Nicholas Ray, and starring Ida Lupino and Robert Ryan. Digital presentation.

A New York detective is living on the edge. Hardened and embittered by years of dealing with the lowest forms of criminal life, to cool off he is assigned a rural murder, where an encounter with a blind woman might turn his life around.

An unusual noir for many reasons. The gritty city scenes give way to snowy pastoral landscapes as Ryan is sent to the country to calm down. There is an early example of hand-held camera as Ryan’s violence is highlighted, and Lupino’s blind woman’s vulnerability is enhanced by Bernard Herrmann’s effective score. A noir to treasure.

events.title: Horror for a Cause – Save the Cinema Museum – Night of the Creeps (1986)
events.description:
Get ready for a spine-chilling night at The Cinema Museum on November 19, 2026 at 7:30 PM (GMT) as we continue our thrilling four-month series celebrating iconic 1980s horror classics!

This instalment features Night of the Creeps (1986), a cult favourite that combines alien terror, college hijinks, and unstoppable zombie fun into one unforgettable retro horror fest. Perfect for fans of 80s genre cinema, this screening promises scares, laughs, and nostalgia all rolled into one.

Every ticket and donation supports the vital campaign to Save the Cinema Museum, ensuring this unique home of film history and community continues to thrive. Join us, bring your friends, and immerse yourself in a night of horror and heart – all for a cause worth fighting for!

events.title: Julien Donkey-Boy (1999) on 35mm
events.description:
Julien Donkey-Boy, 1999, United States

Harmony Korine’s Julien Donkey-Boy follows a schizophrenic young man adrift within a deeply dysfunctional family. Its use of grainy, digital video textures and elliptical, fragmented imagery blends abrasive immediacy with moments of unexpected tenderness. The first Dogme 95 film made outside Europe, which reaffirmed Korine’s singular vision while pushing the movement’s stripped-back aesthetics into new, emotionally resonant territory.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: The Live Ghost Tent – Quarterly Meeting December 2026
events.description:
The Live Ghost Tent – quarterly meeting of The Laurel and Hardy Society.

For this meeting of The Live Ghost Tent, we are excited to introduce Al Friswell, who will give us an informed talk about the link between effects maestro Ray Harryhausen (creator of stop-motion creatures for films including The 7th Voyage of Sinbad and The Clash of The Titans) and comedy duo Laurel and Hardy.

Al, an animator/restorer and artist/sculptor, is the conservator for the Ray and Diana Harryhausen Foundation and he repairs and restores Ray’s wonderful models. Al will relay personal conversations with Ray and his daughter Vanessa Harryhausen on the link between Ray and The Boys. The Live Ghost Tent will follow Al’s talk with screenings of a selection of Laurel and Hardy films that illustrate this link, one of which will be Ray Harryhausen’s favourite Laurel and Hardy film. So come and join us and find out more.

The films we intend to show are:

Flying Elephants (1928), silent short directed by Frank Butler, Hal Roach; Hog Wild (1930), short directed by James Parrott; Busy Bodies (1933), short directed by Lloyd French; and Dirty Work (1933), short directed by Lloyd French.

The meeting runs from 3pm to 7pm.

More details on our Facebook page.

events.title: 80 Years of Martin and Lewis: Artists and Models (1955)
events.description:
Artists and Models (1955) is the most acclaimed of Martin and Lewis’s films, and it’s not difficult to see why.

This eye-popping satire of 1960s moral panic follows struggling painter Rick Todd (Martin) and his roommate, comic-book mad aspiring writer Eugene Fullstack (Lewis). On a mission to find success amidst a bloodthirsty comic book boom, Todd draws inspiration from his roommate’s nightly screaming fits.

Martin and Lewis meet their match alongside powerhouse comic performances from the wonderful Shirley Maclaine (in one of her earliest screen roles) and Dorothy Malone (just one year before her Academy Award winning turn in Douglas Sirk’s Written on the Wind).

Directed by former Looney Tunes cartoonist Frank Tashlin, Artists and Models is jam-packed with visual gags and boundary-pushing innuendo. Lewis thrives under Tashlin’s direction, giving a performance so elastic and extreme that it wouldn’t feel out of place in a Bugs Bunny short.

This film marked the first collaboration of many between Lewis and Tashlin who (beyond his own self-directed oeuvre) quickly became Lewis’s director of choice.

The film will be preceded by an introduction from I’ll Say She Is curator Charlotte Ross.

events.title: Early Colour Live!
events.description: A collaboration between legendary magic lanternists Jeremy and Carolyn Brooker, and the Kennington Bioscope, this unique evening will feature a fantasia of colour from the era of the magic lantern through to early cinema. The Brookers will use an original triunial lantern to show how spectacular and inventive a magic lantern show could be, while Christopher Bird will demonstrate examples of colour in early cinema, including stencil colour, hand-coloured Méliès, and genuine Kinemacolor, the first true colour system, on his hand-cranked 35mm projector, all with musical accompaniment.

events.title: Dracula (1973) and They Have Changed Their Face (1971), introduced by Kim Newman
events.description:
We are delighted that acclaimed author, critic and broadcaster Kim Newman, who ‘cut his teeth’ at the Gothique Film Society, will be joining us to introduce two rare ‘Dracula’ adaptations.

Dracula was presented by the Canadian Broadcasting Company in its Purple Playhouse series, which also included adaptations of Victorian melodramas such as Sweeney Todd and The Bells.

Indeed, this positions Dracula as a theatrical piece, with the count sporting enormous fangs and an English accent, and made up to look like Bram Stoker’s mentor, barn-storming stage actor Henry Irving. Inevitably, the one hour cut-down loses several key characters, but it does add a few interesting thoughts, such as whether the biting of Mina was Jonathan Harker’s doing, after he had been transformed into a vampire in Transylvania.

They Have Changed Their Face is amongst the oddest adaptations of Stoker’s novel, though it takes cues from F.W. Murnau’s Nosferatu and has a crossover with Hammer’s weirdly modish The Satanic Rites of Dracula whereby a wealthy industrialist lives in an isolated mansion (all ‘crumbling horror movie location’ outside but ultra-Moderne all-white inside).

Adolfo Celi, best known as the villain in the Bond film Thunderball, plays the suave industrialist who beckons unsuspecting employees to his ‘lair’. The point that rich and powerful people are like vampires isn’t new, but director Corrado Farina makes it in an unusual way, depicting a Gothically corrupt world which now has a certain retro appeal.

We hope you enjoy these rare and unusual adaptations of a much-told story.
